newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian firms raise cheap debt from global market.
newsitem.headline: Indian firms raise cheap debt from global market.

text.p: Indian firms are tapping the global debt market for funding at low rates as competition increases among foreign banks for a piece of the growing Indian economy, bankers said on Wednesday.
They said the cost of funding has fallen sharply as hard-nosed Indian firms -- state-owned as well as private -- are striking deals cheaper than ever before.
"IRFC (Indian Railway Finance Corporation) raised a seven-year $50 million FRN (floating rate note) at 115 basis points above LIBOR last year," said an official at a European bank in Bombay.
"This year we hear they are raising $150 million at 75 basis points above LIBOR - - a drop of 40 basis points in one year."
State-run IRFC's paper is backed by a letter of comfort, or guarantee, from the ministry of Finance.
But India's blue-chip private firms are striking deals at similar rates without such guarantees, bankers said.
Indian firms are often getting better rates than their counterparts in Southeast Asia, a banker said.
Japanese and Korean banks are now looking at India as the new frontier for growth, making competition more intense.
"They are aggressively chasing commodity financing deals," said a banker. "They are looking for bulk volumes with no restriction on return on capital."

The top arrangers of syndicated cross-border loans for India are ANZ Banking Group, Bank of America, Citicorp, Fuji Bank, Chase Manhattan, State Bank of India, Kredietbank, Dai-Ichi Kangyo Bank, ABN-AMRO Bank and Sanwa Bank, bankers said.
More than 60 foreign banks, not all of them with local offices, are chasing business in India, they said.
"People want to put money in India now," said Jayesh Shah, vice president (finance) at textile firm Arvind Mills.

Indian companies are showing an increasing appetite for cheap offshore funds. They start off with syndicated loans repayable in two to three years followed by seven-year floating rate notes (FRNs) and a bond offering, bankers said.
FRNs and bonds are costlier ways to raise funds but give the company a wider investor base and greater publicity.
These investments come in handy as the company grows and seeks to raise larger amounts of funding from the global market, bankers said.
The government has given a fillip to long-term borrowings by taking FRNs and bonds maturing in 10 years or more out of an annual ceiling on external commercial borrowings.
Some Indian companies contest the claim that India is over-banked.
"Indian firms raise about $7.0 billion a year in foreign debt," said an executive at engineering and construction firm Larsen & Toubro Ltd.
"That's a small amount in the global market," he said.
